forces.title: AI transforming telco operations, shifting equipment demand toward AI-native
forces.description: The pervasive integration of AI agents across telecom customer care, network operations, and software engineering is fundamentally reshaping telcos' operating models. This shift, driven by the desire for productivity gains and cost reduction, will prioritize AI-native solutions over legacy systems. For network equipment manufacturers, this implies a structural change in demand, moving towards hardware and software that natively supports AI-driven automation, predictive maintenance, and smarter network expansion, pushing telcos to invest in new capabilities rather than merely maintaining existing infrastructure.
forces.source_title: AI in Telecom: The Opex Reckoning

forces.title: Sustained CAPEX for 5G SA and fibre expansion drives demand
forces.description: European telecom operators are expected to maintain high capital expenditures in 2026, driven by the critical need to upgrade mobile networks to 5G Standalone (5G SA) and extend fibre broadband to more customers. This continued investment, particularly the reprioritisation of 5G SA after fibre rollouts, represents a significant tailwind for telecom network equipment manufacturers, ensuring a steady order book for RAN, core network, optical transport, and fibre components. Investments in new mobile sites and upgraded antennas also contribute to this demand.
forces.source_title: European telecoms set to see modest growth in 2026

forces.title: Europe's lagging 5G leadership delays advanced equipment adoption
forces.description: Europe is falling behind regions like Asia, USA, and the Middle East in 5G technological leadership, particularly in network speeds and the scaled deployment of 5G Standalone (5G SA) capabilities. This delay is attributed to European telecom companies' struggles with profitability, which leads to postponed investments in cutting-edge technology. For network equipment providers, this represents a headwind, as the slower adoption of advanced 5G SA networks could mean reduced demand for the most innovative and high-value equipment, impacting market growth and technological progression within the region.
forces.source_title: European mobile networks lose ground in the global 5G race

forces.title: IoT and private networks drive new 5G SA revenue streams
forces.description: The rising significance of low-value subscriptions for IoT-based services, coupled with broader service packages for logistics, transportation, and location services, is creating new revenue streams for telecom operators using 5G Standalone (5G SA). Additionally, the expected development of private network use cases, where 5G often outperforms Wi-Fi, provides further opportunities. These evolving service demands directly drive the need for advanced 5G SA network equipment capable of supporting massive machine-type communications and ultra-reliable low-latency communications, creating an upside for manufacturers.
forces.source_title: European mobile networks lose ground in the global 5G race

forces.title: Telcos prioritize AI for CAPEX optimization and network efficiency
forces.description: Telecom operators are increasingly leveraging AI for crucial functions like predictive maintenance and more efficient planning of network expansions. This strategic use of AI, as demonstrated by companies like Deutsche Telekom, allows operators to anticipate hardware failures and optimize investment allocation. For network equipment manufacturers, this is a structural shift, as future products will need to be "smarter" and integrate with AI platforms for real-time data analysis and automation, enabling telcos to reduce operational costs and maximize the efficiency of their capital expenditures.
forces.source_title: How AI could drive growth in European telecoms

forces.title: Fibre network overbuild challenges market efficiency and rollout pace
forces.description: In the Netherlands, the rapid expansion of fibre optic networks has led to "network overbuild" in some areas, where multiple operators (e.g., KPN, Open Dutch Fiber, Delta Fiber) have deployed parallel infrastructure. This competition and redundancy can make it challenging for newer fibre operators to gain market share and sustain profitability, leading some like Delta Fiber and ODF to scale back ambitions. This structural challenge influences the pace and economics of future fibre rollout, impacting demand for new fibre network equipment as operators reconsider investment strategies in saturated zones.
forces.source_title: Fibre will not be the sole broadband technology in the Netherlands

forces.title: Cable broadband defends market share amidst fibre growth
forces.description: Despite the accelerated adoption of fibre broadband in the Netherlands, cable (HFC) solutions have maintained a relatively strong market share at 38%. Operators like VodafoneZiggo are actively upgrading their networks to Docsis 4.0, which, combined with brand, marketing, and ancillary services, allows them to compete effectively against fibre providers even without a speed advantage. This sustained competitiveness from cable limits the complete market dominance of fibre, creating a cyclical dynamic that impacts the rate of fibre equipment demand and prolongs the lifecycle of existing cable infrastructure.
forces.source_title: Fibre will not be the sole broadband technology in the Netherlands

forces.title: Regulatory frameworks limit telco growth, impacting equipment investment
forces.description: The European telecom sector operates within a regulatory framework that limits product and pricing differentiation, and restricts the ability to sell advertisements. This, combined with infrastructure-like returns, leads to growth rates that lag significantly behind large technology platforms. For telecom network equipment providers, this creates a key risk, as the constrained profitability and growth of their primary customers (telecom operators) can limit the budget available for network upgrades and expansion, particularly for non-essential or high-value equipment.
forces.source_title: European telecoms set to see modest growth in 2026

forces.title: Enhanced network reliability demanded by regulators post-outages
forces.description: Following mobile network outages in several European countries in 2025, regulators are expected to increase their focus on network reliability, recognizing telecom's role as critical infrastructure. This regulatory pressure will compel telecom operators to invest more in ensuring the robustness and resilience of their networks. For equipment manufacturers, this translates into a structural demand for more reliable hardware, redundant systems, and advanced network management tools that can prevent outages and ensure service continuity, even if competition makes price increases difficult for telcos.
forces.source_title: European mobile networks lose ground in the global 5G race

forces.title: Expanding Irish broadband and 5G subscriptions drive equipment needs
forces.description: Ireland is experiencing strong growth in broadband and 5G connectivity. Gigabit broadband is available to 88% of premises, with 50% of Fibre-to-the-Premises (FTTP) enabled homes having active service. Furthermore, 5G subscriptions surged by 26% year-on-year to 2.16 million by Q2 2025. This rapid expansion in both fixed and mobile connectivity, coupled with initiatives like the National Broadband Plan, creates a significant tailwind for telecom network equipment manufacturers, as operators continuously invest to meet rising subscriber demand and expand network coverage and capacity.
forces.source_title: Bank of Ireland Sectors Team — Technology, Media and Telecoms (TMT) H1 2025 Insights / H2 2025 Outlook September 2025

forces.title: Satellite-to-device connectivity expands telco coverage opportunities
forces.description: The emergence of direct-to-device satellite services, exemplified by the Vodafone and AST SpaceMobile agreement, aims to provide connectivity to 4G and 5G smartphones in areas lacking traditional mobile or fixed infrastructure across Europe. This technological advancement presents an upside driver for telecom network equipment, as it requires integration with existing terrestrial networks and potentially specialized ground equipment for satellite base stations. While not directly equipment for the satellite itself, the broader ecosystem and enhanced coverage capabilities create opportunities for network evolution and supplementary equipment demand from telecom operators.
forces.source_title: Bank of Ireland Sectors Team — Technology, Media and Telecoms (TMT) H1 2025 Insights / H2 2025 Outlook September 2025

viewpoints.title: Telcos must embrace AI-native operating models to avoid cost-creep
viewpoints.description: Bain views that telecom operators are at a critical juncture, facing significant shifts in operating cost structures due to AI integration. While AI offers automation and augmentation across functions, telcos risk increased operating expenses without proportional productivity gains if they merely bolt AI onto legacy processes. The key is to reshape operating models to be AI-native, focusing on end-to-end workflow redesign and strategic AI compute budgets to achieve faster, simpler, and higher-performing operations, rather than just optimizing old processes. This approach implies a shift in demand towards AI-integrated equipment.
viewpoints.source_title: AI in Telecom: The Opex Reckoning

viewpoints.title: European telecom sector anticipates modest growth but sustained network investment
viewpoints.description: ING Think projects modest 2% revenue growth for the European telecom sector in 2026, driven by new services and price increases, with EBITDA growing slightly faster due to cost rationalisation. Crucially for equipment providers, investments in upgrading mobile networks to 5G Standalone and expanding fibre to more customers are expected to remain high, indicating sustained demand for telecom network equipment. This positive outlook for investment persists despite challenges from competition, new satellite services, and lower Average Revenue Per User (ARPU) in some markets.
viewpoints.source_title: European telecoms set to see modest growth in 2026

viewpoints.title: Europe's 5G leadership lags, potentially delaying advanced equipment adoption
viewpoints.description: ING Think highlights that Europe risks falling behind Asia, the USA, and the Middle East in 5G technological leadership, particularly in network speeds and standalone network deployment. This lag is attributed to European telecom companies' struggles with profitability, potentially delaying investments aimed at achieving technological superiority. While 5G Standalone (5G SA) is expected to become a priority for leading operators, the slower pace compared to other regions could impact the demand for the most advanced 5G network equipment in Europe and limit broader economic productivity enhancements.
viewpoints.source_title: European mobile networks lose ground in the global 5G race

viewpoints.title: AI poised to drive growth and efficiency in European telecoms
viewpoints.description: ING Think views AI as a significant opportunity for European telecom operators, offering dual benefits of cost reduction and enhanced revenue generation. AI is increasingly being applied to customer service, network efficiency, predictive maintenance, and smarter capital expenditure strategies. Operators with clear AI strategies, such as Deutsche Telekom and Swisscom, are well-positioned to lead this transformation. The widespread adoption of AI is expected to improve bottom lines for telcos and facilitate the creation of innovative services, ultimately driving sustainable growth and the evolution towards smarter networks, requiring compatible and advanced network equipment.
viewpoints.source_title: How AI could drive growth in European telecoms
